1. Explain, without using the word “variable”, why “sex” might be a variable in one dataset but a constant in another.

In a general OPD register some records say “male” and others “female”, so sex tells you something that differs from one person to the next. In a dataset of pregnant women every record says “female”. There, sex is identical for every unit, so it carries no information that distinguishes one record from another: it is a constant in that dataset.

2. A field worker records “type of latrine used” and later reports its “mean” across households. What is wrong with that statement, and what should be reported instead?

Type of latrine is qualitative (nominal): “pit latrine” and “flush toilet” are categories, not amounts, so averaging them (or their numeric codes) is meaningless. Report the frequency and percentage of households in each category, and the mode if one typical value is needed.

3. The clinic register holds 100 children and 11 columns. How many data points (cells) does it contain? Classify “age in completed months” and “number of diarrhoeal episodes in the past month” as discrete or continuous, with a reason.

Cells = 100 × 11 = 1,100. Number of diarrhoeal episodes is discrete: it is a count (0, 1, 2 …) and 1.5 episodes is impossible. Age is continuous in nature (time passes continuously); “completed months” is a recording choice that rounds it down to whole months. As recorded, it takes only separate values (12, 13 … 36), so treating it as discrete is also acceptable if you state that it is age in completed months.

1. Without naming the four scales, describe the one extra “permission” each step up the measurement ladder unlocks.

First level: only same or different. Second: adds ordering (higher or lower). Third: adds meaningful subtraction, because gaps are equal. Fourth: adds meaningful division, because zero means none of the quantity.

2. A colleague says “0°C means there is no heat.” Which scale is she confusing Celsius with? Convert 10°C and 20°C to kelvin and compute the true ratio of the two temperatures.

She is treating Celsius (interval: arbitrary zero at the freezing point of water) as a ratio scale. Kelvin starts at absolute zero, so it is a ratio scale:

  1. 10°C = 10 + 273.15 = 283.15 K.
  2. 20°C = 20 + 273.15 = 293.15 K.
  3. Ratio = 293.15 ÷ 283.15 = 1.035.

20°C is about 3.5% “hotter” than 10°C in absolute terms, not twice as hot.

3. In a dataset of 10 children, sex is coded Male = 1, Female = 2, and the “mean sex” comes out as 1.4. What, if anything, does 1.4 tell you?

As a measurement, nothing: the codes are labels. But because sex is binary, the mean of the codes has a hidden meaning. Mean = 1 + (proportion coded 2), so 1.4 = 1 + 0.4: 40% of the children (4 of 10) are girls. The correct report is “4 girls (40%) and 6 boys (60%)”; coding 0/1 would give 0.4 directly as the proportion.

1. A colleague says “if you sampled correctly, the sample mean should equal the population mean exactly.” Is that true?

No. Only a census (sample = population) guarantees that. Any particular random sample gives a statistic (x̄) that usually differs from the parameter (μ) by sampling error, even when the sampling was done perfectly. Correct sampling makes the error unbiased and quantifiable (Chapters 6–7), not zero.

2. Give a population and a sample for a study you might run as a Community Medicine resident, and name which of your numbers is the parameter and which the statistic.

Population: all pregnant women attending antenatal care in the district this year. Sample: the 200 women you interview. The true mean haemoglobin of all of them is the parameter (μ); the mean haemoglobin of your 200 women is the statistic (x̄).

3. In the CBHI survey, 150 of 500 sampled households are members. Compute the membership proportion, give its symbol, and say whether it is a parameter or a statistic. Is the survey dataset primary or secondary data for a resident who reanalyses it five years later?

p̂ = 150 ÷ 500 = 0.30 (30%). It is computed from a sample, so it is a statistic, written p̂; it estimates the population proportion p (written π or P in some texts). For the original survey team the data were primary; for a resident reanalysing them later they are secondary data, collected by someone else for another purpose.

1. List, in order, the steps that turn a raw, unsorted list of 200 haemoglobin readings into something you could read a percentile from.

  1. Start from the raw list. (2) Sort it and choose class intervals with unambiguous limits (e.g. 7.0–7.9, 8.0–8.9 … or half-open classes). (3) Count the frequency in each class (grouped, because 200 readings to 0.1 g/dL have many distinct values). (4) Add relative frequency and cumulative frequency (and cumulative relative frequency). (5) Read or interpolate the percentile from the cumulative relative frequency column, using class boundaries.

2. Why group haemoglobin readings but not “number of children per household”?

Haemoglobin is continuous with many distinct decimal values; listing each would give a table almost as long as the data. Number of children per household takes a few small whole numbers (0, 1, 2, 3 …), so an ungrouped table stays short and loses nothing.

3. Using the diarrhoea table in §1.4.2 (0: 41, 1: 35, 2: 16, 3: 5, 4: 3), compute the cumulative frequency up to 1 episode and the percentage of children with 2 or more episodes.

  1. Cumulative frequency up to 1 episode = 41 + 35 = 76 children.
  2. Children with 2 or more = 16 + 5 + 3 = 24 (equivalently 100 − 76 = 24).
  3. Percentage = 24 ÷ 100 = 24%.

1. Why can a hospital-based cancer registry describe the pattern of cancers among its patients but not the incidence of cancer in the district?

Incidence needs new cases divided by the population they arose from. An HBCR records the patients who came to that hospital, from an undefined catchment and filtered by referral, distance and cost; it has no population denominator. It can say what share of its patients have each cancer site. A population-based registry, which tries to record every new case in a defined area with a census-based population, can give incidence rates.

2. A district’s IDSP data show acute diarrhoeal disease cases doubling this month. Give three explanations other than a true doubling of disease.

  1. Better reporting: more sub-centres or facilities reported this month (completeness rose), or a new private facility started reporting. (2) More care-seeking: a campaign, a new facility or free ORS distribution brought more people to health workers. (3) Artefacts: late reports from last month entered this month, duplicate entries, or a change in case definition or form. Check completeness and timeliness before reading the trend.

3. In a month, 50 primary health centres (PHCs) should report; 44 reports arrive, 36 of them by the deadline. Compute completeness and timeliness (as a share of expected reports).

  1. Completeness = 44 ÷ 50 = 88%.
  2. Timeliness = 36 ÷ 50 = 72% of expected reports (36 ÷ 44 = 81.8% of reports received).

1. A resident surveys 400 randomly chosen women in a block on one day, recording current tobacco use and current hypertension. Name the design and the measure of disease frequency it can give. Why can it not show that tobacco use preceded hypertension?

Cross-sectional survey; it gives the prevalence of hypertension (and of tobacco use) at that time. Exposure and outcome are measured at the same moment, so the survey cannot show which came first; a woman might, for example, have changed her tobacco use after being told she had hypertension.

2. A case-control study of 80 neonatal tetanus cases uses 240 controls. What proportion of the study sample are cases? Why is this not the incidence of neonatal tetanus?

Proportion = 80 ÷ (80 + 240) = 80 ÷ 320 = 25%. The investigator chose 3 controls per case; with 1 control per case the figure would be 50%. The proportion reflects the sampling ratio, not the number of new cases among all births, so it estimates neither incidence nor prevalence.

3. Districts with more mobile phones per household have lower infant mortality. Name the design and the error of concluding that a mother’s phone lowers her own infant’s risk of death.

Ecological study (units are districts). Concluding an individual-level effect from a group-level association is the ecological fallacy: district phone ownership may simply mark wealth, roads and facilities, and within districts the infants who died may have had phones as often as those who survived.

1. Write codebook rows (name, type, values, missing code) for “ever breastfed (yes/no)” and “age at first solid food in months” in an infant-feeding survey.

Variable Label Type (scale) Values / range Missing
ever_bf Ever breastfed binary (nominal) 1 = yes, 0 = no empty cell
age_solids_mo Age at first solid food continuous (ratio), recorded in completed months 0–24 months empty if not recorded; “not yet started” (not applicable) recorded in a separate variable (e.g. solids_started = 1 yes / 0 no), never as 0 or a code in this column

2. In a double-entry comparison of 250 forms with 40 fields each, 30 cells disagree. What percentage of cells disagree, and what do you do with each disagreeing cell?

Cells = 250 × 40 = 10,000. Disagreement = 30 ÷ 10,000 = 0.3%. For each of the 30 cells, pull the original paper form, read the true value, and correct whichever entry is wrong, recording the correction in the cleaning log or script. Cells where both typists made the same error are not caught, which is why range and consistency checks follow.

3. (Optional, R) Why does table(cl$nutritional_status) list “moderate wasting” first if you skip the factor(...) line?

Without the factor(..., levels = ..., ordered = TRUE) line, the column is plain text, and R sorts text alphabetically: “moderate wasting” < “normal” < “severe wasting”. The clinical order (normal < moderate < severe) exists only in your head until you declare it as an ordered factor.
